item.title: The non-residential Bangladeshi: Reform or ruin?
item.description:
There is an old, unwritten law: You can take a Bangladeshi out of the country, but you can rarely extract the country from the Bangladeshi.
When a person steps off a flight at Heathrow or JFK, a silent internal split occurs.
The passport changes, the currency in the wallet shifts, but the underlying psychological software -- that intricate, centuries-old wiring shaped by deltaic floods, agrarian survivalism, and localized territoriality -- remains intact.
This raises an uncomfortable, introspective question: Does life abroad genuinely elevate the non-resident Bangladeshi (NRB) psyche, or does it merely provide a grander, more lucrative stage for domestic vices?
There is a comforting, widely peddled myth popular in living rooms across Dhaka and Chittagong: That the average Bangladeshi, notoriously prone to skipping queues and bribing their way out of trouble back home, magically transforms into a law-abiding saint the moment they step foot into a Western nation.
The argument usually points to the omnipresent "rule of law" -- the strict speed cameras, the unbribable police, the automated tax audits, and the certainty of punishment.
In Bangladesh, institutional fragility turns law into an optional menu of suggestions; abroad, it is assumed, the sheer weight of enforcement forces instant moral reform.
Yet, public record reveals a far more complicated psychological reality. The rule of law certainly creates external compliance, but it does not automatically erase decades of ingrained survival instincts.
For a significant cohort, the presence of a structured, trusting system does not inspire civic duty -- it merely changes the nature of the game.
Where law back home is evaded through brute influence or financial bribes, abroad it is often tested through administrative loophole-hunting, calculated anonymity, and systemic arbitrage.
To trace the psychological shifts of the diaspora, one must look at the historical trail left in the press and legal archives.
The migration waves of the 1980s and 1990s -- particularly to the United Kingdom and Southern Europe -- brought not just workforce muscle, but also the instinctual survival mechanisms of the homeland.
In the late 1980s and through the 1990s, British media periodically highlighted complex welfare and housing benefit scams originating out of East London’s Tower Hamlets -- a hub heavily settled by Sylheti families.
What local authorities framed as sophisticated "social security fraud" was often, at its core, the psychological extension of shonchoy (survival hoarding) and system-gaming honed in a home country where state institutions were meant to be bypassed, not trusted.
By the mid-2010s, investigative operations in Europe laid bare even stranger phenomena: Operations where Bangladeshi migrants holding Italian passports were flying into London on day trips to lodge fraudulent welfare claims before flying back out.
In Australia, immigration reports over the decades have quietly documented cash-in-hand wage undercutting, pseudo-marriages for permanent residency, and localized rental "hot-bedding" schemes run by established diaspora landlords exploiting newly arrived countrymen.
To the foreign observer, these act as felonies or administrative crimes.
But to an introspective Bangladeshi, they are recognizable reflexes.
The rule of law deters blatant chaos, but it cannot prevent the scarcity-driven impulse to extract maximum resources with minimal exposure.
When we look into the mirror, we see ancestral traits that refused to dissolve in foreign waters.
Take the stereotypical Noakhali ethos: Fiercely hardworking, notoriously tight-knit, possessing an innate commercial shrewdness, and an uncompromising loyalty to the clan.
When transported to London’s Brick Lane, New York’s Jackson Heights, or Sydney’s Lakemba, this trait morphs into an enclave mentality.
It creates vibrant business ecosystems, but it can also create isolated echo chambers where Western civil code is treated as an external inconvenience, and the primary moral obligation remains owed strictly to one's immediate lineage back home.
Conversely, consider the Barisal archetype: Deeply opinionated, intellectually pugnacious, and harbouring an ingrained skepticism toward formal authority -- a product of living in a riverine landscape where land itself shifts overnight.
Overseas, this manifests as a refusal to quietly assimilate.
It can express itself as political factionalism -- where Bangladeshi political rivalries are absurdly re-enacted in municipal hall meetings -- or as an instinctive urge to find the hidden loophole in any structured bureaucracy.
Yet, to characterize the NRB experience solely through its missteps is to miss a profound psychological evolution.
Migration is a pressure cooker. While the weak points of the psyche can rupture into criminality under stress, its strengths -- when paired with actual rule of law -- can crystallize into extraordinary global achievement.
For those who genuinely allow the structural stability of foreign nations to alter their internal compass, the transformation is real:
For these individuals, living abroad broke the chain of scarcity mindsets.
It replaced the anxiety of bluffing through life with genuine mastery, allowing the inherent warmth, hospitality, and intelligence of the Bangladeshi character to shine through without the corrupting friction of institutional decay.
Does the non-resident Bangladeshi change for the better or the worse? The truth is that migration acts as a magnifier, not an automatic moral cleanser.
The presence of the rule of law creates a fork in the road rather than a guaranteed transformation.
If a person departs Bangladesh viewing rules merely as obstacles to dodge, foreign soil simply provides a more stable, lucrative infrastructure to game.
The bad gets worse because the safety nets of wealthy nations offer higher stakes to exploit.
However, if a person uses the predictability of foreign law to shed the hyper-vigilance required to survive back home, the Bangladeshi psyche undergoes a remarkable transformation.
The raw energy used for survival converts into an unmatched work ethic. The clannish loyalty expands into genuine civic responsibility.
The NRB remains forever caught between two worlds: Carrying the river's chaos in their blood, while deciding whether to respect or exploit the paved, orderly streets of the world.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Badhan: Those who attacked me are inviting trouble for themselves
item.description:
Actress Azmeri Haque Badhan said on Monday that those who attacked and harassed her in Italy were “inviting trouble for themselves” and called for an end to their “barbaric” behaviour.
“Those carrying out the attacks are, I think, inviting trouble for themselves. Their barbaric behaviour must stop,” Badhon told reporters at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport after returning to Bangladesh from Italy.
Badhon travelled to Italy to attend the Venice Film Festival, where she alleged that a group of expatriate Bangladeshis attacked and harassed her.
“They laid hands on me. I think by doing this, the attackers are making themselves unsafe. What happened in Italy was unfortunate. It has tarnished our image on foreign soil,” she said.
Addressing those who attacked her, Badhon said they might be acting out of loyalty to a political party, but warned that party leaders would not stand by their families if they faced difficulties.
“You are doing this out of love for your party, but when your families suffer, the party leaders will not be there. They are living comfortably and sending video messages,” she said.
Badhan also praised the Italian police for their response, saying she was provided with 24-hour security after the incident and received cooperation from local police and relevant authorities during her stay.
On the night of September 7, Badhan alleged that a group of expatriate Bangladeshis harassed and attacked her while she was staying with family members in Mestre, Italy.
A video of the incident later circulated widely on social media. Various reports said water and soft drinks were thrown at her and that she was physically assaulted.
The video showed several people engaged in a heated exchange with Badhon. She later filed a complaint with the local police, who began analysing video and CCTV footage to identify those involved.
The incident triggered widespread concern over Badhan’s safety in both Bangladesh and Italy. The Bangladesh Embassy and Consulate in Italy said they would provide her with legal and other assistance.
The Bangladesh government also expressed concern and said it would raise the matter strongly with Italy’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

item.title: India women refuse Asia Cup trophy from top Pakistan official after title triumph
item.description:
India’s women refused to collect the Asia Cup trophy from Pakistan Cricket Board chief Mohsin Naqvi on Sunday after beating Sri Lanka by 72 runs in the final to claim a record-extending eighth continental title.
The decision echoed the stance taken by India’s men’s team after winning last year’s Asia Cup, when they also declined to receive the trophy from Naqvi, who is Pakistan’s interior minister as well as chairman of the country’s cricket board and president of the Asian Cricket Council.
India’s players instead celebrated their title without taking part in the formal trophy presentation, as tensions between the two nuclear-armed neighbours again spilled into a major cricketing event.
“That stand has been taken by BCCI (Indian cricket board), and we stand by it,” India coach Amol Muzumdar told reporters.
“We are the champions, that's good enough.”
The presentation ceremony was delayed by nearly 50 minutes before Naqvi handed medals to the Sri Lankan runners-up. The ceremony then ended abruptly, with India’s players presenting medals to each other in the presence of BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia and vice-president Rajeev Shukla.
On the field, India had little trouble securing their eighth Asia Cup crown.
After winning the toss, India posted 183-5, powered by a spectacular opening partnership between Smriti Mandhana and Shafali Verma. Mandhana scored 59 and Verma smashed 68 as the pair added 129 runs in 12.5 overs.
Sri Lanka’s chase began positively, with captain Chamari Athapaththu making 36 and sharing a 58-run partnership with Vishmi Gunaratne, who scored 20.
But Sri Lanka collapsed from 62-1, losing its last nine wickets for just 49 runs. India spinner Shree Charani finished with 4-20 as Sri Lanka were bowled out for 111 from the final ball.
India’s emphatic victory secured the title, but their refusal to accept the trophy from Naqvi became the defining moment of the post-match ceremony.

item.title: Putin urges global youth to change the world together at Ekaterinburg festival
item.description:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has called on young people from around the world to work together to build what he described as a “new, open and just world”, in a televised address marking the opening of the International Festival of Youth in Ekaterinburg.
Addressing around 10,000 young participants representing 191 countries on Sunday, Putin said every nation should have the freedom to determine its own path while enjoying equal access to resources and technology.
“We want every person to remain human and for their fate be determined by things other than nationality, a wallet packed with money, status or background,” Putin said.
“If you share these aspirations, let’s change the world together,” he added, inviting young people to participate in projects in Russia while encouraging them to pursue similar initiatives in their own countries.
Putin welcomed participants to Ekaterinburg, describing the Urals city as a place “where Europe and Asia meet” and highlighting its historic role in Russia’s industrial and intellectual development.
He also referred to the Russian word “mir”, which can mean both “peace” and “world”, saying the dual meaning reflects the character of Russia’s multi-ethnic society.
The festival, running from September 13 to 17, has brought together 5,000 Russian citizens and 5,000 international participants, including 1,000 teenagers aged between 14 and 17.
According to the Federal Agency for Youth Affairs (Rosmolodezh), more than 113,000 applications were submitted from around the world.
Organisers said international applications exceeded those from Russia for the first time in the history of the festival movement, by around 32,000 applications.

item.title: Dhaka air 6th worst in world Monday morning
item.description:
The air quality in Dhaka turned 'unhealthy' on Monday morning, compared with Sunday's 'unhealthy for sensitive groups' level.
Dhaka ranked 6th on the list of cities with the worst air quality in the world this morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 160 at 8:35am.
The air quality was classified as ‘unhealthy’, meaning the concentration of pollutants in the air had reached a level that could pose health risks to the general population, according to the AQI scale.
Singapore topped the list with an AQI score of 169, followed by Malaysia’s Kuala Lumpur with 167 and Indonesia’s Jakarta with 165.
Earlier on Sunday morning, Dhaka ranked 11th among the world’s cities with the worst air quality, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 108 at 9:15 am.
According to the AQI scale, the city's air quality was classified as “unhealthy for sensitive groups”, posing health risks to children, older adults, and people with heart or lung diseases, while the general public is mostly unaffected.
An AQI reading of 101 to 150 is considered ‘unhealthy for sensitive groups’, while 151 to 200 is classified as ‘unhealthy’. A reading between 201 and 300 is considered ‘very unhealthy’, and anything above 301 is categorized as ‘hazardous’, posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides a daily indication of air quality by measuring the level of pollution and its potential impact on human health.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants—particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2), and ozone.
Dhaka has long faced serious air pollution problems, with air quality generally deteriorating during the winter months and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution contributes to around 7 million deaths worldwide every year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer, and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: Can the RMG sector maintain its position in the global apparel market?
item.description:
Bangladesh’s ready-made garment (RMG) industry stands at a critical juncture. The sector generates over 80% of the country’s export earnings while supporting millions of livelihoods. However, global competitiveness now extends beyond cost, quality, and delivery to include sustainability, transparency, responsible business practices, and credible environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance.
The key question is whether Bangladesh can move beyond a compliance-driven mindset and leverage sustainability practices and reporting as strategic tools to strengthen its position in the global apparel market.
The RMG sector transformed significantly after the 2013 Rana Plaza tragedy, which exposed critical weaknesses in workplace safety, labour compliance, and factory governance. In response, the industry adopted widespread reforms supported by global initiatives, regulatory authorities, and international buyers.
These reforms led to significant improvements in workplace safety, structural integrity, labour standards, and environmental management. Bangladesh now hosts the world’s largest number of LEED-certified green garment factories. Many manufacturers have also adopted energy-efficient technologies, wastewater treatment, water recycling, and renewable energy systems, demonstrating the sector’s growing commitment to sustainable manufacturing.
Despite these achievements, Bangladesh operates in an increasingly competitive global apparel market. Increasing competition from Vietnam, India, and Turkey highlights the need to strengthen competitiveness beyond low-cost production. Future success will depend on sustainability performance, innovation, supply-chain transparency, and resilience rather than price alone.
Global sustainability transformation requires organizations to integrate sustainability practices with credible sustainability reporting through a structured five-step roadmap. The process begins with assessment and governance, where organizations identify material ESG risks using double materiality and align priorities with the UN SDGs.
Photo: Courtesy
Next, sustainability is embedded into operations through carbon measurement, Scope 3 emissions management, renewable energy, circular production, labour rights, and supply chain traceability.
These practices respond to evolving global regulations. The roadmap then focuses on performance monitoring using measurable ESG indicators and science-based climate targets (SBTi). Finally, organizations disclose sustainability performance through frameworks such as GRI and SASB supported by external assurance.
Together, sustainability practices and reporting enhance accountability, market access, investor confidence, and the long-term competitiveness of Bangladesh’s RMG sector.
Over the past two decades, sustainability has become a core requirement in global apparel supply chains. International brands increasingly require compliance with standards on labour rights, occupational safety, environmental management, and responsible sourcing.
Frameworks such as GRI, the Higg Index, and ZDHC have accelerated the adoption of cleaner technologies, wastewater treatment, resource-efficient production, and stronger monitoring systems across factories. Industry leaders increasingly recognize that long-term competitiveness depends not only on compliance but also on embedding sustainability into core business strategy.
A key pillar of this transformation is sustainability reporting. Leading Bangladeshi manufacturers have begun publishing sustainability and ESG reports using internationally recognized frameworks. These early adopters reflect growing alignment with global expectations and increasing institutional maturity across the sector.
Sustainability reporting strengthens buyer confidence, improves operational efficiency, supports access to green finance, and enhances risk management. It also enables manufacturers to benchmark performance and identify opportunities for continuous improvement.
However, progress remains uneven across the industry. While large exporters are increasingly adopting structured reporting, many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) still lack the technical expertise, financial resources, and data management systems needed for comprehensive reporting.
As a result, they continue to rely on fragmented disclosures driven by buyer audits, certifications, and compliance requirements.
This gap reduces transparency, limits comparability, and raises concerns about data reliability across the value chain.
Although sustainability reporting is not yet mandatory for all manufacturers, it is expected to become a formal requirement by 2027 as global regulatory frameworks evolve.
Bridging this gap will require coordinated efforts to strengthen technical capacity, improve digital infrastructure, and expand access to affordable green finance.
Despite significant progress, several structural challenges continue to limit the full sustainability transformation of Bangladesh’s RMG industry.
One major challenge is the sector’s continued reliance on fossil-fuel-based energy systems, which restricts large-scale emissions reduction. Although some factories have adopted renewable energy solutions, the national energy structure remains carbon intensive.
Access to green finance is another key constraint, especially for SMEs investing in cleaner technologies, wastewater treatment, and digital reporting systems. High initial costs often delay sustainability investments despite their long-term benefits.
Environmental management practices also vary across the sector. While leading factories use advanced wastewater treatment and chemical management systems, many production clusters still face challenges in textile waste management and circular economy adoption.
Labour-related challenges also remain, including wages, worker representation, skills development, and human rights due diligence. Manufacturers must also navigate complex buyer requirements, certification schemes, and regulatory frameworks, which can increase audit fatigue and compliance costs.
To remain globally competitive, Bangladesh’s RMG sector must move beyond compliance-driven sustainability and establish sustainability as a core business strategy.
This requires stronger governance, improved reporting systems, and integration of ESG priorities into corporate decision-making, risk management, and investment planning.
Wider adoption of global reporting frameworks, independent assurance mechanisms, and digital traceability solutions will be essential to improve transparency, credibility, and data quality across the value chain.
At the same time, an inclusive sustainability transition will require targeted support for SMEs through technical assistance, capacity building, and access to affordable green finance.
Collaboration among manufacturers, global brands, policy-makers, financial institutions, development partners, and academic institutions will be critical to overcome barriers and accelerate industry-wide transformation.
Bangladesh’s RMG industry has demonstrated its ability to adapt by improving workplace safety, strengthening compliance systems, and advancing sustainable factory practices.
However, the next stage of competitiveness will depend on transforming sustainability from a set of operational initiatives into a measurable and strategic advantage.
As global apparel sourcing increasingly prioritizes carbon performance, resource efficiency, transparency, human rights, and accountability, cost competitiveness alone will no longer be sufficient.
The central challenge now for Bangladesh is to institutionalize credible sustainability reporting and ensure that responsible practices are embedded throughout the industry.
By doing so, Bangladesh can strengthen buyer confidence, secure long-term market access, and maintain its position as a global apparel leader.
Mohammad Rabiul Kabir is an associate professor at Stamford University, Bangladesh, and a sustainability and ESG professional.

item.title: Towards stronger ties with France
item.description:
At a time when the Bangladesh economy is experiencing a particularly challenging period, it is more important than ever to strengthen our diplomatic relations with nations.
To that end, the visit of the French Senate delegation and their expressed interest in deeper political engagement with Bangladesh is an important moment, and one that Dhaka should seize with clarity and ambition.
France, beyond being a major European power, is also a strategic actor in global security, climate diplomacy, and development cooperation. Strengthening ties with Paris serves Bangladesh’s long‑term interests, especially as we navigate our economic and social challenges in a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape.
The senators’ remarks signal that France sees Bangladesh as more than a development partner and views it as a country with growing regional influence and a role to play in Indo‑Pacific dynamics.
This recognition matters and opens the door to more robust cooperation in areas where France has deep expertise: defense modernization, renewable energy, climate expertise, digital governance, and higher education.
Bangladesh, for its part, has every reason to welcome this interest. France has been a consistent supporter of Bangladesh, be it the climate agenda, infrastructure development, or being a growing market for Bangladeshi goods.
With Bangladesh eventually needing to shed its LDC tag, stronger political engagement with France can help diversify partnerships, expand trade opportunities, and strengthen diplomatic leverage in the entirety of Europe.
Bangladesh, for its part, must articulate clear priorities, from technology transfer and green energy investment to cultural exchanges. Engagement must also move beyond courtesy visits and translate into structured dialogue, joint initiatives, and long‑term agreements.
Bangladesh has the opportunity to deepen a relationship built on mutual respect and shared global concerns with a major European nation. We must not squander it. Stronger ties with Paris will not only enhance Bangladesh’s international standing but also support its aspirations for sustainable development, climate resilience, and eventually, a more prosperous future.

item.title: Getting serious about dengue prevention
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s inauguration of the three‑month nationwide dengue prevention and cleanliness campaign is a reminder once again that Bangladesh cannot afford complacency when it comes to the disease.
Dengue continues to claim lives while hospitals remain strained, and the next three months are considered the highest‑risk period. The PM’s message is clear and one that ought to have been heeded years ago: Dengue cannot be controlled by mosquito‑killing drives alone; it requires public awareness, daily vigilance, and collective responsibility.
The campaign’s emphasis on keeping surroundings clean and removing stagnant water every day reflects the core truth of dengue prevention. Aedes mosquitoes breed in small, overlooked pockets of water -- flowerpots, rooftop corners, discarded containers, construction sites, and household drains.
No city corporation, no ministry, and no volunteer force can eliminate these breeding grounds without active participation from residents.
The PM’s call for coordinated field‑level activities involving local administrations, volunteers, students, and community groups recognizes that dengue prevention must be woven into everyday life.
Around 25,000 volunteers have reportedly already joined the campaign, and this sort of intent shown is the kind of energy we need to turn this campaign into a success.
Yet, while weekly visits to homes and establishments will help identify breeding sites and raise awareness, their efforts will only succeed if households respond -- by cleaning regularly, checking rooftops and balconies, clearing drains, and refusing to let water accumulate.
The PM’s directive to intensify awareness campaigns across television, mass media, and social media underscores the urgency of changing public behaviour, not just public policy.
We have continued to struggle with dengue because prevention has often been reactive, triggered only after outbreaks worsen. This campaign must mark a shift toward proactive, sustained action.
Dengue is preventable. Bangladesh must prove that it can prevent it.

item.title: DUCSU museum: Jinnah’s photographs added, what else is included and omitted
item.description:
Before the Dhaka University Central Students’ Union (DUCSU) election on 9 September last year, the museum showcased photographs and artefacts depicting major historical movements and struggles of Bangladesh, along with iconic portraits of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.

Following its reopening yesterday, Sunday, significant changes were made to the collection. Sheikh Mujibur Rahman’s solo portraits were removed, whilst three photographs of Pakistan’s founder, Muhammad Ali Jinnah, were added.

However, the three displayed photographs of Muhammad Ali Jinnah were vandalised and torn down today, Monday. In protest against displaying Jinnah’s pictures, activists of the Dhaka University unit Chhatra Federation have hung a photograph, which shows the former Ameer of Jamaat-e-Islami and convicted in cases of crimes against humanity (later deceased) Ghulam Azam being beaten with shoes.

Currently, the DUCSU museum features no solo photographs of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman across sections detailing the 1952 Language Movement, the 1954 United Front election, the 1966 Six-Point Demand, the 1968 Agartala Conspiracy Case, the 1969 Mass Uprising, the 1970 General Election, or the Liberation War of 1971.

However, the section covering 1971 to 1975 includes a photograph of the weddings of Bangabandhu’s two sons in 1974 alongside a newspaper cutting regarding the founding anniversary of the Bangladesh Krishak Sramik Awami League (BAKSAL).

The three photographs of Muhammad Ali Jinnah displayed (until noon) included one from 21 March 1948, showing him delivering a speech at the then Racecourse Maidan (currently Suhrawady Udyan), where he declared Urdu as the sole state language of Pakistan. Another was a group photograph from the 1940 All India Muslim League conference in Lahore, and the third was a news clipping from Pakistan’s Dawn newspaper regarding the 1970 election.

Additionally, the museum features portraits of prominent historical figures including AK Fazlul Huq, Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani, Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy, Rabindranath Tagore, Kazi Nazrul Islam, MAG Osmani, Nawab Salimullah, Ziaur Rahman, and Khaleda Zia.

Why Bangabandhu’s photographs omitted

No photographs highlighting Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman’s pivotal role in Bangladesh’s independence movement have been retained in the museum. Instead, the 1971–1975 section displays photographs of his two sons’ weddings and framed newspaper cuttings featuring his image.

Newspaper cuttings titled “No Opposition Party in Bangladesh” and two images depicting the 1974 famine have also been added.

When asked about the absence of Bangabandhu’s photographs, Fatima Tasnim Juma, the DUCSU Secretary for Liberation War and Movement Affairs involved in the museum’s renovation, told Prothom Alo, “After 5 August 2024, images of ‘all icons of fascism’ were removed. It was not solely my individual decision.”

She claimed that various aspects of Bangabandhu’s political career were integrated during the reorganisation. She stated, “We newly added details regarding the 7 March speech, the Six-Point movement, and photographs of the sector commanders. There are images of Mujib prior to 1971 as well as after 1971.”

Denying the complete removal of solo portraits, she added, “It is incorrect to say there are no solo photos; there is a solo image representing the Six-Point movement, and a wooden artwork depicting the 7 March speech has also been displayed.”

However, a walkthrough of the entire museum revealed no solo photograph of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman related to the Six-Point movement.

Regarding the inclusion of Muhammad Ali Jinnah’s photographs, Fatima Tasnim Juma explained that the images were accompanied by captions contextualising his address at Dhaka University. She stated that the aim was not to glorify Jinnah or portray him favourably, but rather to document historical events in which he was directly involved.

Shift in presentation

Following the renovation, the museum chronicles historical events spanning from the establishment of Dhaka University in 1921 to the Language Movement, the Liberation War, anti-autocracy movements, various socio-political campaigns, and the July Uprising of 2024.

Exhibits include martyrs of the 1952 Language Movement, rare captures of the protests, a portrait of one of the central organisers Pearu Sardar, and the text of Mahbub Ul Alam Choudhury’s poem, “Kandte Asini Phansir Dabi Niye Eshechi” (“I Have Not Come to Weep, I Have Come to Demand Execution”).

The Liberation War section showcases portraits of the 11 Sector Commanders, photographs of the Pakistani military surrender, portraits of martyred intellectuals from Dhaka University, and the seven Bir Sreshtho (highest military awardees). Etched below these exhibits is a relief sculpture of the Liberation War, which includes an image of Bangabandhu.

Exhibits from former President Ziaur Rahman’s era include photographs of canal-digging initiatives, a joint photograph with Khaleda Zia, two images from his wartime service, and a sample ballot paper from the 1978 presidential election.

The section on anti-autocracy protests against HM Ershad features 14 photographs, including the iconic image of martyr Noor Hossain with “Down with Autocracy, Free Democracy” inscribed on his back. It also documents DUCSU’s role in the anti-autocracy movement, lists of martyrs from 1982 to 1990, and images of a shot Martyr Asad being rushed to hospital.

Events post-2009—following the Awami League’s ascension to power—are depicted through photographs of the 2013 Hefazat-e-Islam movement, the Shahbagh protests demanding trials for war criminals, the murders of BUET students Abrar Fahad and Soni, the 2020 anti-Modi (Narendra Modi) protests, and the recent July Uprising. However, no prominent photographs were found representing the period between 1991 and 2009.

The literary section displays portraits of renowned figures including Rabindranath Tagore, Kazi Nazrul Islam, Humayun Ahmed, Jasimuddin, Abul Kashem Fazlul Huq, Munier Choudhury, and Abul Fazal. It also features coverage of Inqilab Mancha convener Shaheed Sharif Osman Hadi, showing his gunshot injuries, the arrival of his remains from Singapore, his funeral prayers, and his burial adjacent to Kazi Nazrul Islam’s grave.

Names of Rabbani and Rashed missing from dashboard

On the dashboard listing historical DUCSU election winners, Nurul Haq Nur is displayed as the Vice President (VP) elected in 2019, but the General Secretary (GS) position remains blank.

Golam Rabbani, former General Secretary of the Bangladesh Chhatra League (now banned), won the GS position in 2019. Following allegations regarding his student status at the time of the election, the current Dhaka University administration declared the GS post vacant and subsequently named Rashed Khan (currently Advisor to the Prime Minister) to the position.

Addressing this issue, Fatima Tasnim Juma stated that the matter remains under dispute. Although passed by the University Syndicate, there are no specific governing rules for such a decision. Furthermore, Golam Rabbani’s tenure as GS remains questioned. Consequently, the position is being left blank until a resolution is reached.

She added that regulations do not permit appointing a new candidate to the position after the term has expired. Given the ongoing controversy and ambiguity, the spot remains vacant and will be updated once resolved.

item.title: Those blinded by conventional party politics could act like this: Golam Porwar on tearing down of Jinnah’s photo
item.description:
Commenting on the tearing down of photographs of Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the former Governor-General of Pakistan, from the DUCSU (Dhaka University Central Students’ Union) museum, Jamaat-e-Islami Secretary General Mia Golam Porwar stated that only those blinded by conventional party politics could behave in such a manner.

Earlier today, Monday, student Abu Taiyab Habildar tore down three photographs of Muhammad Ali Jinnah from the DUCSU museum in protest.

Speaking to journalists, he said, “The Jinnah who spoke against our mother tongue, the Jinnah who ordered the arrest of students at Dhaka University’s Curzon Hall in 1948, cannot have a place in DUCSU.”

When asked about the incident during an event, the Jamaat Secretary General remarked, "We have been informed of this. We would say that those who are ignorant of the political history of Bangladesh, those who do not know the historical background of Bangladesh’s creation, and those who do not know who fought and contributed to the liberation and independence of this land—those who lack knowledge of this political history and are merely blinded by conventional party politics—are the ones capable of such behaviour.”

Student tears down Jinnah’s pictures from DUCSU museum

“All patriotic citizens of this land were aligned with the movement he led and the cause he spoke for. People need to understand this history. Political immaturity leads to many actions and responsibilities that raise questions among the public,” Mia Golam Porwar added.

Mia Golam Porwar made these remarks as the chief guest at a Sirat-un-Nabi (PBUH) conference organised by the National Doctors Forum, Dhaka City South, held this afternoon at the Institution of Diploma Engineers, Bangladesh (IDEB) auditorium in Kakrail, Dhaka.

Jinnah’s photos at DUCSU museum: DU administration to take action against those responsible

Following the event, he addressed journalists and answered various queries.

Some in govt envious of peaceful long march

The Jamaat-e-Islami secretary general claimed that certain individuals within the government have grown envious due to the peaceful nature of the Opposition’s Long March.

“They (the government) assumed the Long March would lead to violence, sabotage, arson, and vandalism. They made provocative statements to incite trouble during this peaceful programme. However, the Opposition will not fall for any provocation,” he stated.

In response to a query, the Jamaat secretary general said, “Had the government conceded to the Opposition's demands, there would have been no need for a Long March. A Long March is a recognised political programme in Bangladesh's democratic society. When the incumbent prime minister’s mother (Khaleda Zia) was in Opposition, Jamaat, as part of an alliance, participated alongside the BNP in a Long March that she led. Why and when a Long March becomes necessary is something those in power fail to grasp; it is understood only when one is in the Opposition.”

Chhatra Federation hangs image of Ghulam Azam being beaten, in protest of Jinnah photos at DUCSU museum

Criticising the prime minister’s statement that “if issues could be resolved through a Long March, the government itself would have conducted one,” Mia Golam Porwar remarked that such words were unbefitting of his position.

He noted that the Opposition took the statement poorly, and the public found it inappropriate.

The Jamaat Secretary General assured that the Opposition's Long March towards Rangpur would remain peaceful. He called upon all parties—including the government, police administration, and political organisations—to cooperate with the Long March, expressing hope that they would receive support to ensure its peaceful execution, as in previous instances.

The keynote speaker at the conference was Mufti Mahmudul Hasan. The event was chaired by Maruf Shahriar, President of the National Doctors Forum (NDF), Dhaka City South.

Other speakers included Shafiqul Islam Masud, Secretary of Jamaat's Dhaka City South unit, and NDF Secretary Mahmud Hossain, among others.

item.title: Jamaat secretary indicates its candidates for Dhaka’s two city corporations
item.description:
The Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami has yet to formally announce its candidates for the Dhaka North and Dhaka South city corporation elections. However, the party’s secretary general, Mia Golam Porwar, has indicated who is likely to contest the elections for the party.

Mia Golam Porwar spoke about the matter in response to questions from journalists after an event at the Institution of Diploma Engineers, Bangladesh (IDEB) auditorium in Kakrail, Dhaka, on Monday afternoon.

Earlier, he addressed the Sirat-un-Nabi conference organised by the National Doctors Forum’s Dhaka South unit as the chief guest.

After the conference, responding to a question from a journalist, Mia Golam Porwar said Jamaat had made organisational preparations to contest local government elections. The process of finalising candidates for union, upazila, district and city corporation elections is already at an advanced stage. Candidates have also been internally announced in many areas, he said.

Mia Golam Porwar said Jamaat would contest the elections to both Dhaka city corporations, adding that the party had already selected its candidates organisationally. However, they had not yet been formally announced, and the candidates would be declared at an appropriate time.

Meanwhile, reports have already emerged in the media that Jamaat is set to nominate Selim Uddin for Dhaka North and Shadik Kayem for Dhaka South.

The Election Commission has yet to announce the dates for the Dhaka North and Dhaka South city corporation elections. Political parties, however, have already begun selecting candidates ahead of the polls.

At a press conference yesterday, the National Citizen Party (NCP) announced that it would nominate Nasiruddin Patwary as its mayoral candidate in Dhaka South and Asif Mahmud Sajib Bhuyain in Dhaka North.

item.title: Police Superintendent suspended after drug detected in test
item.description:
Police Superintendent (TR) AFM Nizam Uddin of the Police Headquarters has been suspended from government service after he was found to be positive in a “dope test”.

He was attached to the office of the deputy inspector general (DIG) of the Rangpur Range.

The Ministry of Home Affairs issued a notification to this effect on 10 September. According to the notification, Nizam Uddin had gone to the Police Headquarters on 8 January to attend the ‘DSCSC-2026’ course at Mirpur Cantonment. He fell ill on 7 June while the course was under way and was sent to the Combined Military Hospital (CMH) in Dhaka.

The notification said that, on the advice of specialist physicians, Nizam Uddin underwent a “dope test” as part of further medical examinations. The test returned a positive result, which was deemed contrary to the discipline of the course.

Under the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 2018, Nizam Uddin was suspended from government service, the notification said.

It added that he would receive a subsistence allowance in accordance with the rules during his suspension.

The order, issued in the public interest, will take immediate effect, according to the notification.

Jinnah’s photos at DUCSU museum: DU administration to take action against those responsible
item.description:
The Dhaka University administration has decided to take action against the individuals involved in displaying photographs of Pakistan's former Governor-General Muhammad Ali Jinnah and the then-Chhatra Sangha leader Abdul Malek at the Dhaka University Central Students’ Union (DUCSU) museum.

Dhaka University Vice-Chancellor Professor ABM Obaidul Islam confirmed to Prothom Alo that an investigation committee has been formed for this purpose, with Pro-Vice-Chancellor (Administration) Professor Mohammed Almujaddade Alfasane serving as its convener.

The university will also investigate two other issues related to DUCSU. The launch of a teacher evaluation website without university authorisation and the installation of a monument named "Nirbhik July" in front of the Central Library without permission.

The university administration issued a statement regarding these matters on Monday through the Public Relations Office.

The statement noted that several news reports concerning DUCSU have come to the university authorities' attention. These activities are inconsistent with the university's established laws, regulations, policies and administrative structure.

According to Article 24(a) of the Dhaka University Order, 1973, the responsibility for the supervision, maintenance and control of university property is vested in the Syndicate.

Additionally, according to the notes under Section 4 of Chapter 14 of the Dhaka University Ordinance and Statutes, the student union must make any decision subject to the guidance of the Vice-Chancellor.

The statement emphasised that the "Nirbhik July" monument, installed by DUCSU on the west side of the Arts Building and in front of the Central Library, was done without any permission or consultation with the Syndicate or the Vice-Chancellor, which is beyond their jurisdiction under university law.

The university’s statement further declared that displaying photographs of Pakistan's then-Governor-General Muhammad Ali Jinnah and then-Chhatra Sangha leader Abdul Malek in the DUCSU museum conflicts with the history of the Language Movement and Bangladesh's independence.

It stated that displaying such images in the university museum is in no way acceptable and strict administrative action will be taken against those involved in accordance with university regulations.

Regarding the teacher evaluation website launched by DUCSU without approval, the statement called it inconsistent with university policy and institutional processes.

It noted that teacher evaluation is a vital academic and institutional matter. No individual, organisation or student union can launch an independent evaluation system on their own. The statement also pointed out that the website exposes teachers' personal information, which is a punishable offense under the law.

The statement asserted that there is no scope for establishing any form of ‘dual administration’ at the university. While DUCSU is an important student representative body, all of its activities must be conducted within the university’s laws, regulations, policies and administrative framework.

The administration warned that any attempt to bypass university authority or establish a parallel structure will be strictly resisted.

Vice-Chancellor ABM Obaidul Islam told Prothom Alo that he was not informed beforehand about the displaying of the photographs or the other initiatives taken by DUCSU.

He added that necessary actions will be taken based on the findings of the investigation committee's report.

item.title: Chhatra Federation hangs image of Ghulam Azam being beaten, in protest of Jinnah photos at DUCSU museum
item.description:
In protest against the display of Muhammad Ali Jinnah’s photographs at the museum of the Dhaka University Central Students’ Union (DUCSU), leaders and activists of the Dhaka University unit of the Bangladesh Chhatra Federation have hung a photograph showing Ghulam Azam being beaten with shoes at the museum.

A group of students led by Arko Barua, organising secretary of the Chhatra Federation’s university unit, put up the photograph at around 3:00 pm on Monday.

At the museum, it was seen that a photograph showing Ghulam Azam being beaten with shoes at Baitul Mukarram in 1981 had been placed at the spot where Jinnah’s photograph had been displayed.

Arko Barua, organising secretary of the Bangladesh Chhatra Federation’s Dhaka University unit, said, “DUCSU is not anyone’s personal property. No one will accept a one-sided presentation of history. And because of what people like Ghulam Azam did in 1971, people beat him with shoes in the 1980s. We have preserved the history of the people of this country.”

He further said, “Yesterday, Juma (DUCSU’s Liberation War and Democratic Movement affairs secretary) said that they had put up Jinnah’s photograph because they wanted to. In exactly the same way, we wanted to put up a photograph of Ghulam Azam, so we did.”

DUCSU reopened the museum on Sunday following renovation work. It did not include a standalone or prominent photograph of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, the leader of Bangladesh’s independence struggle. Instead, three new photographs of Pakistan’s founder, Muhammad Ali Jinnah, were added.

One of them shows Jinnah speaking at an event at the then Racecourse Maidan, now Suhrawardy Udyan, Dhaka, on 21 March 1948, where he declared, “Only Urdu will be the state language of Pakistan.”

Another is a group photograph from the All-India Muslim League’s annual conference held in Lahore in March 1940, in which Jinnah appears. The third is a newspaper clipping from Pakistan’s Dawn carrying a photograph of Jinnah in a report on the 1970 election.

Students express anger

The display of Muhammad Ali Jinnah’s photographs at the DUCSU museum has sparked discussion and criticism on social media.

Shahriar Mustaq, a resident student of Muktijoddha Ziaur Rahman Hall, wrote on Facebook, “How much longer will it take for this DUCSU to develop love for the Bangla language and Bangladesh? The photograph of someone who opposed Bangla as a state language has been given a place in the DUCSU museum!”

Imdadul Haque, a student of Salimullah Muslim Hall, wrote, “Once, DUCSU fought for an independent Bangladesh; now it is fighting to protect anti-national forces!”

Chhatra Dal protests

The Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal (JCD) has also protested against the display of a controversial 1948 photograph of Muhammad Ali Jinnah at the DUCSU museum. The organisation issued a statement on Monday, 14 September, expressing its opposition.

It alleged that Jinnah’s photograph had been displayed at the museum in a manner that conflicts with the history of the Language Movement and the struggle for independence.

The organisation demanded that the photograph be removed and that DUCSU stop being used as a platform for promoting the ideology of any particular political group.

Chhatra Union demands restoration of Mujib’s photograph

On the same day, the Bangladesh Chhatra Union protested against the addition of Muhammad Ali Jinnah’s photograph and the removal of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman’s photograph from the DUCSU museum.

In a statement, the organisation said removing Sheikh Mujibur Rahman’s photograph, as a leader of the independence struggle, from the museum amounted to distorting history.

It warned that students would take appropriate action unless Jinnah’s photograph was removed and Sheikh Mujibur Rahman’s photograph was restored promptly.

item.title: DU warns Ducsu against ‘parallel administration’, threatens action
item.description:
Dhaka University authorities have warned the Dhaka University Central Students’ Union (Ducsu) against creating any “parallel” administrative structure, threatening disciplinary action over several recent initiatives that they say violated university rules and bypassed its administrative authority.
In a statement issued on Monday, the university raised objections to an unauthorized July uprising memorial erected by Ducsu, the display of photographs of Muhammad Ali Jinnah and Abdul Malek in the Ducsu gallery, and the launch of a separate website for evaluating university teachers.
The authorities said there was “no scope for establishing a dual administration” at the university and that Ducsu, despite being an important representative body of students, must conduct its activities within the university’s existing laws, rules, policies and administrative framework.
“Any attempt to establish a parallel structure or process by bypassing the university’s administrative authority will be strictly resisted,” the statement said.
The university said Ducsu erected a memorial named “Nirbhik July” on the western side of the Ducsu building, adjacent to the Arts Building and in front of the Central Library, without consulting or obtaining permission from the Syndicate or Vice-Chancellor.
Citing Section 24(A) of the Dhaka University Order, 1973, the authorities said responsibility for the supervision, maintenance and control of university property rests with the Syndicate.
They also referred to provisions of the Dhaka University Ordinances and Regulations, saying decisions of the students’ union are subject to directives from the Vice-Chancellor.
On that basis, the university said the construction of the monument without approval fell outside Ducsu’s jurisdiction.
The authorities, however, stressed that the university administration supported the spirit of the July Mass Uprising.
They said the foundation stone of the university’s planned “July Memorial Monument” was inaugurated at Mall Chattar on August 5 by the Vice-Chancellor in the presence of members of the university community and families of those killed in the uprising.
The university also objected to the display of photographs of Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the then governor-general of Pakistan, and Abdul Malek, identified in the statement as a leader of the then Chhatra Sangha, in the Ducsu gallery.
The authorities described the display of photographs of individuals whose actions they said conflicted with the history of the Language Movement and Bangladesh’s independence as “entirely unacceptable” in the gallery.
The statement said strict administrative action would be taken against those responsible in accordance with university rules and regulations.
The university also criticized Ducsu for launching a website to evaluate teachers without authorization, saying the initiative was inconsistent with established university policies and institutional procedures.
Teacher evaluation is an academic and institutional matter, and no individual, organization or students’ union can independently introduce a separate evaluation mechanism, according to the statement.
The authorities also alleged that the website had made teachers’ personal information publicly accessible, describing such disclosure as a punishable offence under the law.
Dhaka University said it already has a teacher evaluation policy approved at the university’s highest level and that the system is currently being implemented.
The authorities therefore rejected the introduction of any separate evaluation mechanism outside the approved framework, arguing that such initiatives could undermine the university’s institutional processes and reputation.
The statement described the Ducsu activities in question as “unwanted, unexpected and unacceptable.”
The university said it would not compromise on institutional discipline or what it described as preserving the dignity of the history of Bangladesh’s Language Movement and Liberation War.
It warned that unauthorized construction or attempts to establish separate administrative systems without university approval would result in administrative action against those responsible under existing regulations.

item.title: Islami Bank protest turns violent, 25 reportedly injured
item.description:
At least 25 people were reportedly injured as two groups clashed outside Islami Bank Bangladesh’s headquarters in Motijheel on Monday during a demonstration demanding changes to the bank’s board and an end to alleged interference by S Alam Group.
The violence, involving scuffles and a chase and counter-chase, erupted in front of Islami Bank Tower as the Islami Bank Conscious Customers’ Forum gathered for a protest over the bank’s governance.
Among those injured was businessman Motasim Billah, vice-president of the forum. The organization said the injured were taken to different hospitals in Dhaka for treatment.
Eyewitnesses said an altercation broke out between two groups over the scheduled demonstration and quickly escalated into pushing and scuffling before both sides chased each other.
The forum later held a press conference at the scene, alleging that former Islami Bank employees dismissed over alleged irregularities in recruitment and people linked to S Alam Group had gathered there before its program began.
Professor Nur Nabi Manik, president of the forum, alleged that the group attacked customers and shareholders as the demonstration got underway.
He claimed at least 25 forum members were injured.
Manik also alleged that forum members were forcibly removed in the presence of police but that law enforcers failed to take effective action.
He presented photographs and video footage to journalists in support of the forum’s account.
No immediate comment was available from the former employees or others accused by the forum, and their role in the violence could not be independently verified.
The forum said Monday’s demonstration was called to demand the appointment of “honest, competent and professional” individuals to Islami Bank’s board of directors and to oppose what it described as continued “sinister interference” by S Alam Group.
Manik said the forum had been campaigning peacefully around a seven-point set of demands intended to safeguard the deposits of Islami Bank’s approximately 30 million customers.
“The Islami Bank Conscious Customers Forum is an apolitical organization. We have been campaigning through systematic and peaceful means, pressing for a seven-point list of demands aimed at ensuring the security of deposits belonging to Islami Bank’s approximately 30 million customers,” he said.
“But today’s attack cannot be dismissed as a minor incident.”
He alleged that the incident indicated the continued influence of S Alam Group.
At the press conference, forum leaders further alleged that some people previously dismissed from the bank over recruitment irregularities, as well as leaders and activists associated with the Awami League, Chhatra League and Jubo League, were involved in the attack.
The allegations could not immediately be independently verified, while those accused were unavailable for comment.
The forum demanded that authorities identify those responsible by examining CCTV footage from the area as well as videos recorded by journalists and others during the clash.
It called for the immediate arrest and prosecution of those found responsible.
The forum said its demonstrations would continue until its demands concerning deposit security and good governance at Islami Bank were addressed.

item.title: State minister: Shyamoli TB Hospital to become national TB institute
item.description:
The 250-bed TB Hospital in Dhaka’s Shyamoli will soon be upgraded to the National Institute and Hospital for Tuberculosis Control, said Primary and Mass Education State Minister and hospital management committee Chairman Bobby Hajjaj.
He said the upgrade would expand facilities for tuberculosis diagnosis, treatment, research and training while strengthening the hospital’s overall capacity.
“Necessary initiatives have been taken to develop the hospital into a modern, integrated and effective institution for tuberculosis control,” he said.
Bobby Hajjaj made the comments as the chief guest at a meeting of the hospital management committee at the hospital’s conference room on Monday.
The state minister said steps would be taken to fill vacant posts for doctors, officials and employees as soon as possible.
Addressing the manpower shortage was essential to improve the quality of services and make the hospital’s operations more effective, he said, adding that the necessary measures would be taken in consultation with the Ministry of Health.
He also said an initiative would be taken to construct a new 500-bed building to expand the hospital’s services and capacity.
Bobby Hajjaj instructed the relevant authorities to remove encroachments from the footpath in front of the hospital to ensure unobstructed movement for patients and the public.
During his visit, the state minister inspected different wards and spoke with patients, attendants, doctors, nurses and other healthcare workers about the hospital’s services and challenges.
He also sought updates on cleanliness, medicine supplies and other facilities and instructed officials to take necessary measures to improve the hospital’s overall services.
“Every patient who comes to a government hospital for treatment must be treated with humanity and responsibility. The hospital authorities must give the highest priority to ensuring that patients do not face any kind of suffering or inconvenience,” Bobby Hajjaj said.
The meeting was chaired by Dr Ayesha Akter, member secretary of the hospital management committee and deputy director of the hospital.
Officials from the Ministry of Health, Directorate General of Health Services and Department of Social Services, members of the hospital management committee, health reporters, doctors, officials and employees of the hospital attended the meeting.

item.title: Verdict in case against Quader, Arafat, 5 others Tuesday
item.description:
The International Crimes Tribunal is set to deliver its verdict on Tuesday against seven accused, including Awami League General Secretary Obaidul Quader, former state minister for information and broadcasting Mohammad Ali Arafat, and five others in a case involving alleged crimes against humanity committed during the July mass uprising in 2024.
A three-member bench of International Crimes Tribunal-2, headed by Justice Nazrul Islam Chowdhury, fixed the date on Monday.
The other members of the bench are Judge Md Manzurul Bashid and Judge Nur Mohammad Shahriar Kabir.
Prosecutors Gazi MH Tamim, Faruk Ahmed and other members of the prosecution team were present at the tribunal.
The tribunal had earlier kept the case reserved for judgment after hearing closing arguments from both the prosecution and defence. Tribunal-2 passed the order on August 17.
State-appointed lawyers M Hasan Imam and Ishrat Jahan represented the accused, while prosecutors Mizanul Islam and Gazi MH Tamim represented the prosecution.
Besides Obaidul Quader and Mohammad Ali Arafat, the other accused are Awami League Joint General Secretary AFM Bahauddin Nasim, Jubo League President Sheikh Fazle Shams Parash, and General Secretary Mainul Hossain Khan Nikhil, Chhatra League President Saddam Hossain and General Secretary Wali Asif Enan.
All seven accused are absconding.
On January 22, Tribunal-2 ordered the trial to begin after framing charges against the seven accused. The tribunal took cognisance of the formal charges the prosecution submitted on December 18, 2025.
The prosecution began presenting its closing arguments on August 4.
According to the prosecution, the accused jointly issued directives and made provocative and inciting statements to suppress the July-August movement.
They allegedly held several meetings to plan violence and called on party activists to take to the streets and put up resistance.
The prosecution further alleged that the accused were involved in armed attacks, harsh repression and efforts to control the media in some areas.
It said their actions resulted in killings, attempted killings and widespread violence across the country, which constitute crimes against humanity.

item.title: Family alleges medical negligence in infant’s death at Dhaka hospital
item.description:
The family of a nine-month-old infant has alleged that medical negligence led to the child’s death at Padma General Hospital in the capital.
A relative raised the allegation during a Facebook Live session late Sunday night, claiming that no doctor was available when the child’s condition deteriorated in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU).
The hospital, however, denied the allegation, saying the child died of cardiac arrest.
The relatives said nine-month-old Ayan Abdullah was admitted to Padma General Hospital on September 1.
The child’s mother alleged that when his condition worsened while he was receiving treatment in the PICU, repeated attempts to call a doctor went unanswered.
“If a child dies right now—if their breathing stops—what happens to them? The child had developed complications beforehand. My allegation is that this occurred precisely because of negligence in duty,” she said.
The relatives also alleged that no doctor was available near their ward.
“There were no doctors in the vicinity of our ward. We went to the doctors’ room nearby. There are several doctors’ rooms; we checked those too. There wasn’t a doctor anywhere. There wasn’t even a doctor from the NICU present,” they said.
Dr Nazmul Haque, a medical officer at the hospital, said the child died of cardiac arrest. He said the child had remained stable until around 8pm but stopped breathing around 9pm.
Dr Md Atiqul Islam, a consultant at the hospital, said he was informed about the situation during the night.
“I asked if my presence was required, but the hospital told me it wasn’t anything serious,” he said.
Zahirul Islam Anik, an administrative officer at Padma General Hospital, said the allegation could be checked through CCTV footage.
“Whether a doctor was present or not can be verified by checking the CCTV footage. We will investigate the matter. We have doctors and nurses on duty 24 hours a day,” he said.
He denied the allegation of medical negligence.

item.title: Rain likely in parts of country
item.description:

item.title: Application filed to stay Grameen Kalyan’s Tk666 crore tax verdict
item.description:
An application has been filed seeking a stay on the High Court verdict ordering Grameen Kalyan, an entity owned by Dr Muhammad Yunus, to pay Tk666 crore in tax arrears claimed by the National Board of Revenue (NBR).
The application was filed on Monday with the Chamber Judge Court of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court.
On September 10, the High Court ruled that Grameen Kalyan must pay Tk666 crore in taxes claimed by the NBR.
A High Court bench led by Justice Md Mozibur Rahman Miah delivered the verdict after dismissing a rule issued in response to a writ petition challenging the tax demand.
Barristers Abdullah Al Mamun and Fida M Kamal represented Dr Yunus in court.
Earlier, following the July mass uprising, the High Court had withdrawn, on its own initiative, a verdict ordering Grameen Kalyan to pay the Tk666 crore claimed by the NBR.
The withdrawal order was issued by a bench comprising Justice Mohammad Khurshid Alam Sarkar and Justice Sardar Md Rashed Jahangir. The case records were subsequently sent to the chief justice.
The case was later referred to a new bench for hearing.
Grameen Kalyan had filed two separate writ petitions in 2017 challenging tax demands for the 2012-13, 2013-14, 2014-15, 2015-16 and 2016-17 fiscal years following a reassessment.
The court initially issued a rule after a preliminary hearing. A later High Court bench dismissed the rule, effectively upholding the NBR's tax demands.
Lawyers said the dismissal of the writ petitions means the NBR can now collect the amount from Grameen Kalyan as income tax.

item.title: SP suspended after positive drug test
item.description:
Superintendent of police (TR) AFM Nizam Uddin has been temporarily suspended from government service after his urine sample tested positive for benzodiazepines and amphetamine/methamphetamine.
An order to this effect was issued on Monday through a notification signed by Senior Secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs Manzur Morshed Chowdhury. The notification was signed on September 10.
According to the notification, Nizam Uddin is currently attached to the office of the Deputy Inspector General (DIG) of Rangpur Range. He left Police Headquarters on January 8 to attend the DSCSC-2026 course at Mirpur Cantonment.
During the course, he fell ill on June 7 and was taken to the Combined Military Hospital (CMH) in Dhaka. On the advice of specialist doctors, he underwent a drug test as part of his medical examinations.
His urine sample tested positive for benzodiazepines (BZO) and amphetamine/methamphetamine.
The notification said the test results were contrary to the discipline required for the DSCSC course. Under the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, such conduct constitutes misconduct and is punishable under the rules.
In view of this, Nizam Uddin was temporarily suspended from government service with effect from August 31 under the relevant provisions of the rules.
During the suspension, he will be entitled to a subsistence allowance in accordance with government rules. The order, issued in the public interest, took effect immediately.

item.title: Reading South Asia through its women
item.description:
South Asian Stories of Women Writers (in Bangla, Narir Kolome Dokkhin Asiar Golpo ), a compilation of short stories, is a portrayal of women’s lives and their struggles in societies they live. The book, at the length of 624 pages, presents such a panorama of wonderful stories!
The book includes as many as 28 short stories written by the writers of Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan, Pakistan, and Afghanistan. It is bilingual; every short story has two versions--Bangla and English.
Stories originally written in Bangla have been translated into English and vice versa. Therefore, a host of translators, alongside fiction writers, have significantly contributed to the publication.
From Bangladesh came fourteen stories written by fourteen distinguished writers, including Mokbula Manzur, Rizia Rahman, Niaz Zaman, Selina Hossain, Purabi Basu, and Nasreen Jahan.
The contributors themselves span generations and borders: established names sit alongside emerging voices, and each represented country contributes its own set of authors, together forming a chorus that is polyphonic in style but consistent in its underlying concerns.
The editors, Nur Quamrun Naher and Rokeya Islam, are themselves fiction writers, and their own stories have naturally earned a place in the volume.
How are South Asian societies, and how can they be connected through literature?
Societies are different, but women face more or less the same problems—discrimination and repression. They are often marginalized and put to troubles by the patriarchal apparatus.
Stories of women are as appealing as men. They possess distinctive taste and tone. Women writers writing on women’s problems become more truthful, and readers should like the feminine focus.
The stories are interesting in themselves.
In “Primordial” by Mokbula Manzur, we find a fury in a village woman, Saburan, who punishes her husband, Suruj, for the crime of selling her younger sister to a brothel.
“Ensnaring Birds” by Selina Hossain centers on the rape of a minor girl and the attempts of two journalists to find the real criminals.
Nasreen Jahan in “The Stranger” brings up the issue of the existence of Halala marriage in the Muslim community. Here divorced Kusum is wooed by her rogue (ex)husband, Hafiz, to come back to him, but the religious rule does not allow it.
To legalize a comeback, it is necessary for the divorced woman to be wed to another man who will divorce her again. Accordingly, Kusum is wed with a beggar, but things go awry. Kusum decides to stay with the beggar, avoiding Hafiz.
The book carries the mark of the brilliance of writers, of translators, and of editors. The writers, packed together, talk in a polyphonic voice on women's issues.
The plots are varied, but they share the same sentiment--no injustice to women. Therefore, the narratives have a feminist undertone.
Women demand respect and recognition in society. They are in constant competition and conflict with men.
The stories in the book point to gender binary and drive human conscience towards a humane existence. It is set to play its own role for creating consciousness of women's rights and raising its voice against any form of gender discrimination.
The book may provide a pleasant reading experience for the general readers. And it will be a particularly useful compendium for the researchers interested in South Asian women writers and writings.
Dr Binoy Barman teaches English at Daffodil International University and serves as Executive Editor of the Journal of Society and Progress (JSP).

item.title: IM10 FC win both titles in inaugural Futsal League Bangladesh
item.description:
